title: Workhorse: digit-sum rule from a single congruence
content: digitSum_rule_of_modEq_one shows that whenever 10^k ≡ 1 (mod d) with d ≥ 2, the base B = 10^k validates the digit-sum rule: d ∣ n ↔ d ∣ (digits (10^k) n).sum. The proof extracts 10^k % d = 1 from the congruence (using 1 % d = 1 for d ≥ 2) and feeds it to Mathlib's Nat.modEq_digits_sum, then converts the resulting ModEq into an iff via Nat.ModEq.dvd_iff.
mathContext: If $B \equiv 1 \pmod d$ then $B^j \equiv 1 \pmod d$ for all $j$, so $n = \sum_j a_j B^j \equiv \sum_j a_j \pmod d$; hence $d \mid n$ iff $d$ divides the base-$B$ digit sum. Every divisibility-by-digit-sum rule is an instance of this one congruence.

title: Main theorem: existence for every coprime modulus
content: exists_pow_ten_digitSum_rule is the resolution of the parent's open question: for every d ≥ 2 coprime to 10 there is a positive exponent k such that 10^k is a valid digit-sum base. The witness is k = φ(d), supplied by the Fermat–Euler theorem Nat.ModEq.pow_totient, with positivity from Nat.totient_pos. digitSum_rule_pow_totient records the explicit base 10^{φ(d)}.
mathContext: Euler's theorem states $a^{\varphi(d)} \equiv 1 \pmod d$ whenever $\gcd(a,d)=1$. Taking $a = 10$ gives $10^{\varphi(d)} \equiv 1 \pmod d$, so $B = 10^{\varphi(d)}$ always works. This proves existence for the whole class of moduli coprime to 10 in one stroke, subsuming the parent's individually proved rules.

title: Sharp characterization via the multiplicative order
content: pow_modEq_one_iff_order_dvd proves 10^k ≡ 1 (mod d) ↔ orderOf (10 : ZMod d) ∣ k by transporting the congruence into ZMod d (ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff) and applying orderOf_dvd_iff_pow_eq_one. orderOf_ten_pos then shows the order is positive for coprime d: it divides φ(d), and φ(d) > 0 rules out order 0.
mathContext: In the finite ring $\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}$, the residue of $10$ is a unit exactly when $\gcd(10,d)=1$, and its multiplicative order $\mathrm{ord}_d(10)$ is finite. A power $10^k \equiv 1 \pmod d$ precisely when $\mathrm{ord}_d(10) \mid k$ — the valid exponents form the subgroup generated by the order.

title: Minimality: the smallest working base is 10^{ord_d(10)}
content: orderOf_least_valid_exponent bundles three facts: ord_d(10) > 0, it is itself a valid exponent (10^{ord_d(10)} ≡ 1 (mod d)), and it is ≤ every positive valid exponent (Nat.le_of_dvd applied to the order-divisibility characterization). minimal_pow_ten_digitSum_rule then states that the base 10^{ord_d(10)} validates the digit-sum rule, exhibiting the smallest power-of-10 base that works.
mathContext: Since every valid exponent is a multiple of $\mathrm{ord}_d(10)$, the least positive one is the order itself, and the minimal power-of-10 digit-sum base is $10^{\mathrm{ord}_d(10)}$. For example $\mathrm{ord}_3(10)=1$ (base $10$), $\mathrm{ord}_{27}(10)=\mathrm{ord}_{37}(10)=3$ (base $10^3$), and $\mathrm{ord}_7(10)=\mathrm{ord}_{13}(10)=6$ (base $10^6$).
prerequisites: Divisibility and the least element of a subgroup of ℤ

title: Concrete instances, including new base-10^6 rules for 7 and 13
content: Five corollaries of digitSum_rule_of_modEq_one: 3 (base 10), 7 and 13 (base 10^6), 27 and 37 (base 10^3). Each discharges its congruence 10^k ≡ 1 (mod d) by kernel decide over ℕ-arithmetic. The rules for 7 and 13 are new relative to the parent, which obtained 7 and 13 only via truncation methods rather than a genuine base-10 digit-sum rule.
mathContext: $\mathrm{ord}_7(10)=6$ because $10^6 = 1000000 \equiv 1 \pmod 7$ and no smaller positive power of $10$ is $\equiv 1$; likewise $\mathrm{ord}_{13}(10)=6$. So summing the six-digit blocks of $n$ detects divisibility by $7$ and by $13$ — a uniform digit-sum rule replacing the ad hoc truncation tricks.
